Cc: support@edgeops.com

Subject: VPC tunnel orchestration & fallback playbook

Hi Avery / Naomi,

Thanks again for taking time yesterday. Per our conversation, attached are the initial diagrams and a short draft playbook that shows how EdgeOps expects to orchestrate encrypted site-to-site tunnels to your VPCs and the recommended fallback behaviors when a primary tunnel or control-plane route is degraded. High level:

- Control plane: managed BGP session over the primary tunnel; route advertisements limited to customer-prefixes only.
- Data plane: encrypted GRE/IPsec tunnels with MTU 1400 for path MTU safety across cloud/colo hops.
- Fallback: automated secondary tunnel via the backup fabric + deterministic route-preference change; if BGP is down, fall back to a statically pinned egress via our out-of-band proxy.

Attachments: vpc-tunnel-diagram.pdf (diagram), fallback-playbook.md (draft).

Can your team review the tunnel termination point recommendations and the proposed NAT behavior for tenant egress? We called out two options in the playbook (preserve source vs. NAT to tenant-egress-PAT).

Best,
Tom
EdgeOps Solutions

Tom / team —

Thanks for the materials. Quick read-through and a few questions up-front before the engineering deep-dive:

1) Tunnel MTU: 1400 is sensible as a conservative default. We need to capture the impact on our KV cache replication payloads (some RPCs push >1200 bytes). Karithik, can you validate whether 1400 will cause fragmentation for common inference workloads?

2) BGP timers & route-preference: we prefer a deterministic failover window <= 45s for the customer-facing SLA. Can EdgeOps guarantee BGP hold/timers that align to that? If not, we need the fallback to kick earlier (e.g., local route-preference change after 20s).

3) NAT semantics: for auditability we prefer source-preserving where possible and NAT only for egress to third-party aggregators. We need an ops-mode that allows toggling. Is that exposed in your control plane?

I'll schedule a 40-minute sync with the infra team tomorrow. Naomi — can you pull the staging traffic profiles? Tom — we'll iterate the playbook after ops review.

Cheers,
Avery

Redwood Inference

Following up with a quick technical read — flagged inline notes in the diagram PDF and a couple of suggested changes:

- MTU: 1400 is OK but for our largest payloads (model shard syncs and KV cache checkpoints) we see bursts up to ~1500 bytes once headers are added. Two options: increase MTU to 1450 and enable MSS clamping at the host, or keep 1400 and enable application-side chunking for checkpoint transfer. I recommend option A for lower CPU overhead on the proxy.

- BGP hold timers: set minimum hold-time to 30s with aggressive keepalives (10s) on the primary. For the failover, implement a local router-policy that flips next-hop-preference after 18s of lost keepalives — reduces customer impact. EdgeOps should expose a timer knob in the orchestration API.

- Health checks: add an application-layer HTTP health probe from our edge to the customer's control-plane agent on port 2149 (auth token). If probe fails for 12s consecutive, mark path degraded and start secondary tunnel establishment. This reduces false positives from transient packet loss.

- NAT: agree with Avery — prefer source-preserving. For third-party egress, do PAT at the proxy and emit a 1:1 mapping log to the observability sink (s3://redwood-ops/audit/edgeops-nat).

- Observability: add a Prometheus export of tunnel-latency (p50/p95) and BGP session flaps to the shared EdgeOps dashboard. Suggest the Grafana link be included in the playbook.

I'll attach a short diff to the diagram PDF with callouts.

Karthik
Senior Network Engineer, Redwood Inference
